The relatively short intrauterine development, coupled with the small birth mass, suggests a strategy of producing moderately precocial young that can transition quickly to independence. By the time they reach weaning, offspring have more than tripled their birth mass, attaining an average wet weight of 30.3 grams [Wwx = 30.3 grams] approximately 24 days after birth [tx = approximately 24 days after birth], a developmental milestone achieved at the same core temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. This tripling of body mass over a three-week period is fueled entirely by maternal milk, as pups exhibit no solid food ingestion until after the eyes open and exploratory behaviors commence. Juveniles that successfully navigate this transition then enter a prolonged growth phase during which they must accumulate sufficient body reserves to withstand the seasonal food shortages typical of their xeric environment. The weaning weight itself, at approximately one-fifth of the adult asymptotic mass, places these young at a vulnerable stage where predation risk remains elevated.

Growth continues steadily through the juvenile period, with individuals ultimately reaching an asymptotic adult body mass of 145 grams [Wwi = 145 grams], a figure that represents the maximum recorded wet weight for healthy, free-living adults. This ultimate body size places Dipodomys spectabilis among the larger members of its genus, a distinction that carries ecological implications for burrow construction, territory defense, and metabolic demands. The pronounced increase from the weaning weight to the adult mass - roughly a fivefold gain - occurs over several months as subadults hone their seed-harvesting skills and establish independent caches. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that this growth trajectory is relatively rapid, likely facilitated by the high-quality seed resources available in the bunchgrass communities these animals inhabit. As body mass approaches the asymptotic value, the energetic demands of somatic growth diminish and resources become increasingly allocated toward the maintenance of the large, complex burrow systems that are a hallmark of this species’ ecology.

Under thermoneutral conditions, the species exhibits a maximum lifespan of approximately 12.7 years [am = approximately 12.7 years] at 37 °C [T = 37 °C], a remarkably long duration for a rodent of this body size and one that likely reflects the protective benefits of a fossorial lifestyle. This extended longevity, which far exceeds that of most similarly sized small mammals, is thought to be linked to the reduced predation risk afforded by elaborate subterranean burrows and the ability to buffer against extreme surface temperatures. Such a lifespan strategy is consistent with a slow life-history pace, characterized by delayed reproduction, small litters, and substantial parental investment. The survival advantage provided by burrow living may also allow individuals to accumulate extensive experience in locating and storing patchy seed resources, further enhancing their reproductive potential over the years. This relatively rapid attainment of reproductive capability - occurring within roughly four months - allows young born early in the breeding season to potentially contribute to reproduction later that same year, although most individuals likely defer their first breeding attempt until the following season. The onset of gonadal activity coincides with the period when subadults have nearly completed their growth, ensuring that energetic resources can be directed toward the demanding processes of spermatogenesis or oogenesis without compromising somatic development.
